描述_ZN: Page of "The Fairy Riding a Luan", Song dynasty, on silk, color on paper, 25.3 cm in length and 26.2 cm in width.　　No mark of the author. The opposite panel is inscribed in ink by Geng Zhaozhong of the Qing Dynasty: "The style of the painting is high and elegant, with the posture of the sky and the dust. Geng Zhaozhong, Xiangping, inscribed." Inscriptions of Geng Zhaozhong's "True Appreciation", "Qianning Wang's Sons and Daughters Forever", "Dancheng", "Seal of Duke Geng's Painting and Calligraphy ", "Collection of Duke Xin", "Precious Secret", "Yi'er's descendants", "Gong " and other identification and collection seals, a total of 17 parties.　　The picture depicts a luan phoenix flying on wings amidst thin clouds and light mist, with a nymph on its back gazing blankly back at the full moon behind her. The artist has portrayed the depression of the fairy at the moment of looking back vividly, making the originally monotonous scene extremely interesting and giving people an imagination. The fairy's eyes are invisible, but the author uses them to create an intrinsic echo between the moon and the luan and the phoenix, giving the picture an airy and coherent integrity. By depicting the fairy's sash fluttering backward, the artist suggests the invisible wind, and in this way indicates the speed and strong sense of motion of the phoenix as it flies, forming a contrast between motion and stillness with the full moon.　　In terms of the portrayal of the figures, the shape of the nymphs is a departure from the rich and robust physique of the Sui and Tang dynasties, showing the reasonable proportion and proportionality of the female figure.　　The old title of this painting and the inscription of Geng Zhaozhong on the frame both say that the author is Zhou Wenru of the Fifth Dynasty. Zhou Wenji was influenced by the calligraphy of Li Yu, the later lord of the Southern Tang Dynasty, and liked to paint with a thin, straight, and quivering brushwork, with lines that are twisting and turning, and soft in the midst of rigidity. The lines of this painting are as delicate as a spring silkworm spitting silk, with rigidity in the midst of softness, which is not in line with Zhou Wenji's brushwork, so it should be the work of an unknown artist of the Song Dynasty.　　Song painting book" photocopy, Qing Pang Yuanji "Xuzhai famous painting record" recorded.
